1:
Who these oppressors were is settled first. Ellicott traces Midian to Abraham by Keturah and to the rich nomad tribes east of Moab, notes that Moses lived forty years among them, and recalls why Israel was bound to deadly hostility with the nation — the shameful worship of Baal-peor into which, at Balaam's instigation, the Midianites had tempted them. Clarke calls them among the most ancient and inveterate of Israel's enemies, places them on the eastern shore of the Dead Sea with Arnon for their capital, and recalls that they were once all but wiped out. Gill dates the relapse: Deborah and Barak kept the nation to pure worship while they lived, and their death was followed by a return to the Amorite gods.

Henry finds the choice of scourge humiliating. Israel had smarted often enough already, yet a burnt child that dreads the fire went back to it — a revolting rebellious heart, held neither by terror nor by gratitude. And the instrument was despicable. No king, lord or general is named on the Midianite side; the force that ruined Israel was an undisciplined mob, drawn from a people everyone else thought uncultivated. Worse, Israel had subdued and nearly destroyed this very nation two centuries before, and the poor remains had so multiplied that God could move his people to jealousy by those who were not a people.

The raiding followed a pattern, and three of them describe it. Gill notes that the invaders left Israel alone through winter and seedtime, so that the ground was manured and sown; Ellicott adds the cruel logic — living by idleness and plunder, they let others grow the corn and came themselves to reap it — and finds the same in Alyattes, king of Lydia, who left the houses of Miletus standing only so their owners would plough and sow again. He carries it into his own century: the Fellahîn still sow in dread of the Bedouin, their villages abounding in huge underground hiding-places for corn and valuables. Clarke likewise has the raiders arrive early and watch the ripening fields. Keil and Delitzsch reconstruct the route — over the Jordan near Beisan, through the plain of Jezreel, then westward across the country to the coast at Gaza.

The dens and caves are read carefully by Keil and Delitzsch. The definite article shows these were known refuges still standing when the book was written, and though the text says Israel made them, that does not deny the natural caverns of the limestone hills, since the verb covers using a cave as well as digging one. Clarke draws the picture: driven from the plain, the people lived like wild beasts and were hunted like them. Henry blames their own faint-heartedness, calling flight the effect of a guilty conscience — sin dispirits men and sends them sneaking into dens and caves, and a day is coming when chief captains and mighty men will call in vain to rocks and mountains to hide them.

Their numbers get the strongest language. Ellicott prefers locusts to grasshoppers, notes that the Bedouin themselves call locusts the host of God, remarks that camels were very uncommon in Palestine and must have come from the eastern deserts, and treats innumerable as oriental hyperbole — a Bedouin asked by Burckhardt how many brothers he had threw a handful of sand into the air and said, equally numberless.

What was left of Israel afterwards Ellicott renders from the Greek as reduced to pauperism, the Hebrew suggesting flaccidity — a door hanging loose on its hinges, a sere leaf shaking on a tree. Henry sees exact justice in it: they had withheld their substance from God in tithes and offerings and prepared it for Baal instead, so an enemy came to take it away in its season. Only then did they cry to the Lord, crying to Baal having ruined and not helped them.
7:
What Israel cried about, and what God answered, are not the same thing. Gill puts the mismatch bluntly: they cried on account of Midianite oppression, not of the sins that had brought it, of which they seemed to have no sense at all — yet God, meaning to deliver them, sent a messenger at once to give them that sense and prepare them. Keil and Delitzsch describe the same intention as a sequence: before helping he reproved, so that the people might recognise in the misery crushing them a chastisement for apostasy, and repent by remembering what grace had formerly done for them.

Henry finds encouragement in the cry being heard at all. They had neglected God in prosperity, courted his rivals, and turned to him only when driven by extremity; and still, on their complaint, he intended relief — which shows how ready he is to forgive and how inclinable to hear prayer. He reads the order of God's acts as a promise. Before sending an angel to raise up a saviour, God sent a prophet to convict them of sin, so that their crying might carry confession and not merely complaint. We have reason to hope God designs mercy, Henry concludes, when we find him preparing us for it; and furnishing a land with faithful ministers is itself a token for good.

Who the prophet was nobody can say, and the guess on offer is contested. Ellicott notes that Jewish legend names Phinehas son of Eleazar, and remarks how freely the Hagadah supplies names for anonymous prophets — Iddo for the man at Bethel, Jonah for the young man who anointed Jehu. Clarke reports the same tradition and prefers some teacher raised up for the purpose, one of the witnesses God sent from time to time to declare his counsel. Gill rejects the identification on chronology: Phinehas could hardly have lived more than two centuries, and had he been alive it is remarkable that nothing was heard of him under the preceding judges. Both stress that the Hebrew says a man, a prophet — not an angel, as in the earlier chapter — and Ellicott guesses the audience may have been a feast-day assembly.

The message is a recital of favours. Keil and Delitzsch and Henry give it the same shape: God brought them out of Egypt, delivered them from every oppressor, drove those enemies out before them, and gave them the land. Gill adds the moment at the sea, where the pursuing Egyptians overtook them in utmost distress and salvation was wrought. Henry draws two inferences. That God once delivered them from all oppressors implies their present bondage owes nothing to want of power or goodwill in him, but to their having sold themselves by iniquity, so that he would not redeem them until repentance revoked the bargain. And the gift of the land both aggravates their ingratitude and clears God of blame for what has since befallen them.

What was required in return Henry calls easy and equitable. Do not worship the gods of the Amorites — do not court them for fear of what they might do, since what harm can they do while I am your God? Fear God, and you need not fear them. Ellicott identifies those Amorites as the highlanders of Palestine and the most powerful of the Canaanite tribes, their name serving at times for all the rest.

The indictment is a single clause, which Henry and Ellicott both make the hinge. You have not obeyed my voice is short, Henry says, but comprehensive, since disobedience to God is the malignity of all sin — and repentance is genuine only when that, rather than the trouble sin brings, is what we chiefly lament. Ellicott states the principle the chapter turns on: no deliverance can be promised until repentance has begun, and when the prophet's warnings are heeded the deliverer's mission starts.
11:
Who the visitor was is agreed, and Ellicott is impatient with the alternative. A prophet like the one a few verses back he calls obviously absurd: the word there is nabi, here the messenger of Jehovah. Josephus, reporting that a phantasm stood by Gideon in the shape of a youth, is only dressing the story for Gentile readers as usual. Gill identifies him — not a created angel but the Angel of Jehovah's presence, the Word and Son of God, who is expressly called Jehovah in the passage. Henry agrees, adding on Bishop Patrick's authority that these appearances in human shape were a prelude to the incarnation, when God would take our nature for good and all. Keil and Delitzsch describe the guise chosen this time: a traveller with a staff in his hand.

The place is described with some care and located with none. Ellicott prefers terebinth to oak and takes it for a well-known tree beside the altar at Ophrah; Keil and Delitzsch point out that it was the town and not the tree that belonged to Joash, since it is later called Ophrah of the Abi-ezrite, to distinguish it from the Ophrah in Benjamin. Abiezer they identify as a small family in Manasseh, of which Joash was probably head and so lord of the place. On where it stood they part: Ellicott puts it in western Manasseh, following Van de Velde for Erfai near Ephraim's northern border; Clarke places it in the half tribe beyond Jordan; Keil and Delitzsch decline to settle it. Ellicott adds the meanings of two names — Ophrah is fawn and Gideon is hewer.

What Gideon was doing, and where, everyone lingers over. Clarke explains the oddity of the site: a threshing-floor could not be used in open day for fear of the Midianites, who came and carried off the grain as soon as it was beaten out, so Gideon fetched a few sheaves from the field to be threshed privately — and since the country's distress meant there was no vintage, a winepress was the last place raiders would look for corn. Ellicott adds the mechanics, preferring beating out to threshing, since a winepress was a vat sunk in the ground with hardly room for the regular process, and renders the phrase for hiding it literally as making it fly. The open circular floors in the fields, he notes, were where an invader foraged first.

Clarke observes that Gideon is not the only man taken from farm work to command an army and deliver his country: Shamgar was plainly a ploughman who killed Philistines with an ox-goad, and Cincinnatus was fetched from the plough to be dictator of Rome — a case Clarke thinks strikingly like this one.

Henry reads the circumstances of the meeting as three lessons. Gideon was alone, and God often manifests himself to his people out of the noise and hurry of the world, silence and solitude befriending communion with him. He was employed, beating wheat with a rod, probably because there was too little to be worth treading with oxen; a man of account with servants of his own, he would not live in idleness, and honest business puts us in the way of divine visits — as the shepherds had the tidings of Christ's birth while keeping their flocks. And he was distressed, hiding by the winepress like the rest, so the angel came to a man who could speak feelingly of the yoke, the day of greatest distress being God's time to appear for his people's relief. From threshing corn, Henry says, he is fetched to thresh the Midianites.

Henry adds two notes on the man rather than the moment. Joash was alive but passed over, keeping up the worship of Baal in his own household; and the judges had hitherto been raised out of the tribe that suffered most, as here again.
12:
The approach is quiet, and Gill marks the moment it changes. The visitor had waited some while under the oak; Gideon, intent on his work, took no notice of him; so he came forward and stood before him, in his sight.

Then comes the greeting, and Ellicott counts it out — three words in the Hebrew, Jehovah immekâ, Gibbor — and observes that this was once an ordinary salutation and blessing. Clarke prefers the Targum's reverent form of it: the Word of the Lord is with thee, thou mighty man of valour. Keil and Delitzsch read the whole address as promise rather than compliment. It pledged that the Lord would be with him, and that by the Lord's strength he would prove the brave hero he was called; and that pledge was to guarantee him both vigour and victory in the struggle with Midian ahead.

The title itself is evidence about Gideon's past, and two of them press it. Clarke infers that he had already given proof of courage and personal prowess on earlier occasions, which would go far to explain why his countrymen afterwards trusted him. Ellicott doubts the words can refer merely to the energy of his flail, and points out that only the second and third epochs of his life are narrated, the rest surviving in scattered glimpses: that he and his brothers had perhaps fought on Mount Tabor, perhaps even in the older struggle against the Canaanites, so scanty are the details and so uncertain the chronology; that he was of kingly presence; that he had a youthful son, many slaves, and an armour-bearer of his own. Clarke turns the observation into a rule about calling. God picks instruments whom his workings in nature and providence have already fitted for the purpose; they look unlikely, and prove the best qualified for the employment.

Gideon's reply is not the reply of a man who knows what he is talking to. Gill says he took the speaker for no angel but some illustrious and eminent person, and Ellicott makes the title he used a bare courtesy — adoni, the equivalent of the Greek word our translators render sir in the resurrection chapter of the fourth Gospel. He saw only a stranger seated beneath the terebinth that shaded the rock-hewn vat where he was labouring.

Keil and Delitzsch describe the answer as doubting rather than defiant. Pray, sir, if Jehovah is with us, why has all this befallen us? — words that call up the sentence of Deuteronomy asking whether these evils have not come because God is not among us. While knocking out his wheat, they suggest, Gideon had been turning over his nation's misery and the likeliest means of ending it, and could see no possibility of rescue anywhere; which is exactly why the salutation was unintelligible to him.

Ellicott hears the same brooding under the phrase all this — an echo of thoughts about his country and his brothers that had been darkening him through the hard work — and quotes the bitter turn Josephus gives it: a mighty indication of God's favour to me, that I am forced to use this wine-press instead of a threshing-floor. The rest of the complaint he traces to the psalms that ask where the old wonders are and how long the Lord will forget, and to the warning that if you forsake him he will forsake you. Clarke's verdict on the speech is that it is remarkable for energy and simplicity, and that the despondency in it goes no further than the case warranted.
14:
A look does the work of an argument here, and the commentators dwell on it. Gill has Jehovah himself — the same person just called his angel — gaze earnestly at Gideon and smile on him, showing that he bore him kindness and meant him well. Ellicott points out that the speaker now talks as the Lord, exactly as in the visit to Abraham, and that many have drawn the obvious inference: no created angel but the angel of the covenant, the captain of the Lord's host. The only other course open is to treat him as merely the mouth of God. The looking Ellicott takes literally, though it carries favour and acceptance with it, as the Vulgate's respexit suggests; and the look, he says, put fresh force into the man. He also explains why the Greek translators keep the angel of the Lord all through: a thorough Alexandrian distaste for anthropomorphism, for any phrase that seemed to lower the unapproachable majesty of God.

Keil and Delitzsch account for the change of name in the narrative on the same ground — the reply itself manifests the speaker as Jehovah, above all in that closing question, which echoes so plainly the commissioning of Moses at the bush. Go in this thy strength means the strength Gideon has at that moment, because Jehovah is with him and can still work wonders as in the fathers' days; the demonstrative points back to what the promise has just conferred.

Gideon's second objection is of another temper than his first. Keil and Delitzsch note that he now perceives he is not dealing with a man: he stops calling rescue impossible and asks only by what means, conscious of his own smallness and his family's. Here Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch divide over one vowel. Ellicott observes that our translators deliberately read adoni again, a mere courtesy, on the ground that Gideon did not fully recognise his visitor until the disappearance, whereas the Hebrew manuscripts read Adonai, Lord — and if that is right, Gideon is already addressing God as the source of the message. Keil and Delitzsch simply take the second reading.

What Gideon pleads is his household. His family is literally his thousand, and Clarke gives the arithmetic behind it: tribes were divided anciently into tens, fifties, hundreds and thousands, so a thousand marked a grand division and a numerous kindred, and Gideon means that his own has dwindled — or, if the word is a shortened plural, that the thousands in Manasseh are thinned and the tribe can do little against its enemies. Ellicott renders the adjective the meanest rather than poor, the article requiring it, and compares the way David is called the little one among his brethren; what had brought the house of Abiezer so low is unknown, though the overbearing pride of Ephraim may have had a hand in it. Least in his father's house, he adds, Gideon was also last of it, his brothers having all been killed. Such diffidence at the outset Ellicott finds regularly in men God chooses.

The answer is the promise repeated, and Gill quotes the Targum for it — my Word shall be thy help — which he thinks meets every plea of meanness, unworthiness and weakness at once. Keil and Delitzsch gloss smiting Midian as one man to mean at a single blow, in the manner of killing one person; Clarke offers both readings, that Gideon should overcome the whole host as surely as if he had one man to fight, or else destroy them to a man.
17:
Having been promised everything, Gideon asks for proof of it, and Gill notes the oddity of the plea. The grace he asks to have found he has evidently found already — it showed in the salutation that called him a man of might, in the charge laid on him, and in the pledge of help and success that followed. Ellicott adds that the expression is found both in the Old and New Testament, and paraphrases what is really being requested: some clear proof that this is no mere vision, that the message truly comes from God, and that it means him well.

What kind of proof, the three of them put differently. Clarke wants an outright miracle, one that would satisfy Gideon that his visitor had wisdom and power enough to authorise him for such a task and to fit him for it. Keil and Delitzsch argue that after the promise Gideon could no longer doubt that the words were spoken in God's name, so the sign is asked for something narrower — an assurance that the speaker was himself God, as he had implied; and they note that the Hebrew turn of phrase is borrowed from the language of everyday conversation rather than from anything liturgical.

With the request goes a second one, and it is the hospitable kind. Do not leave this spot, Gideon says, until I have come back and set my offering before you; and Keil and Delitzsch observe that the stranger consents on the instant, promising to stay until he returned. Gill takes the errand at face value — he was going to his father's house for food to entertain the visitor with, and wanted him kept where he was in the meantime.

The word Gideon used for what he was fetching carries more freight than the errand does. Ellicott points out that minchah means an offering, and above all an offering made to God, since that is its constant use in the sacrificial law for the meal-offering of flour; the Greek accordingly turns his sentence into a promise to sacrifice before him. Yet he thinks the neutral word was chosen deliberately: Gideon suspected, without yet being persuaded, that the man beneath the terebinth was more than a man, and simple hospitality was still mixed in with his deepening awe. Keil and Delitzsch weigh the term more heavily — not a sacrifice in the technical sense, and not a present of food either, but a gift laid before God, upon whose acceptance or refusal the whole question of the sign would turn. Clarke leans the other way. A minchah was commonly bread, wine, oil and flour; the asking of it suggests Gideon took the stranger for a divine person; but what he actually made ready and carried out looks like nothing more than a meal set before a guest of consequence.
19:
The meal is described in enough detail that Clarke can match it against living custom. Dr Shaw's account of Arab entertainment supplies the pattern: a bowl of milk and a basket of figs, raisins or dates set before the arriving guest to stay his appetite, then a kid or goat, lamb or sheep fetched from the flock according to the size of the company, half of it seethed at once by the host's wife and served with cucasoe, the remainder cut up and roasted as kab-ab against the next day's breakfast. On Harmer's suggestion Clarke reads the verse the same way — a slight refreshment offered first to the supposed prophet, with a request that he wait for something better; then the kid killed, part of it stewed and brought out in a pot with the unleavened cakes Gideon had baked, and the roasted part packed in a basket for the traveller to eat further along his road. Where it was carried Clarke also fills in: probably to a tent, whose shade and the oak's together kept off the sun without shutting out the breeze, since Arabs still receive their guests under cover in the open air.

Ellicott attends to the ingredients and the measure. The cakes were unleavened because that was the quickest bread to make, as when Lot baked for the angels and the witch of Endor for Saul. The ephah of flour he reckons at about twenty-two and a half pounds, where a homer would have been enough, an ephah being ten of them — but Eastern hospitality holds nothing too lavish. On the verb for presenting it he splits the difference between the Greek manuscripts: approached, in the Vatican copy, is too weak, and worshipped, in the others, too strong, the sense lying between the two at offered with respect and reverence.

What follows is not a dinner, and Gill marks the refusal: rather than sit down to what had been prepared, the visitor issued instructions. Clarke states the purpose plainly — the flesh and bread were to become an offering to God, the broth a libation. Ellicott notices that the speaker is here, and only here in the chapter, the angel of Elohim rather than of Jehovah; renders the direction as pointing to yonder crag, the living rock making a serviceable altar; and gathers parallels for the pouring: the drink offering poured out as a libation in the Genesis narrative, the sea-water Elijah poured over his sacrifice to make deception impossible, and the thick water called Naphthai which Nehemiah poured on the offering, when the sun shone out and a great fire kindled and every man marvelled.

The staff is the last of the traveller's props. Gill remarks that the visitor had been walking with it, which is part of why Gideon pressed food on him before he should go on his way; Ellicott calls it the ordinary equipment of an Eastern traveller. Clarke describes the touch and its effect — the flesh touched, fire rising out of the rock, the offering consumed — and calls it the most evident proof of supernatural agency; Keil and Delitzsch say simply that in the miracle Gideon got the sign he had asked for, that his visitor was God. Ellicott sets the flame among its fellows as the usual token of God's presence and of his acceptance of an offering, and draws the contrast out of the rock itself: water comes from it for man's blessing, fire to show that God is there. He notes what the text does not say — that the angel went up in the flame, as happens in the later chapter. And Clarke adds that the disappearance ended nothing: God went on speaking with Gideon, whether by secret impression on his heart or by a voice he could hear.
22:
Recognition arrives too late to be comfortable. Gill has Gideon work it out from the miracle and from the manner of the departure; Ellicott says the last sign gave him a far deeper sense of the grandeur of his visitor than anything before it. What follows is a cry rather than a sentence. Clarke calls it elliptical, the natural speech of a distressed mind, and supplies what is missing — have mercy on me, else I die, for I have seen an angel of Jehovah face to face. Ellicott holds that nothing need be supplied, though the alarm shows well enough what the fear was; he corrects the rendering to for to this end have I seen him. Keil and Delitzsch describe the exclamation itself as one Hebrew uses both for grief over a calamity already fallen and for dread of one expected, and place this firmly in the second class: fear of dying.

That the fear was ordinary rather than eccentric is a point all three press. Clarke reports it as a settled sentiment before the law and under it, that whoever saw God or his representative angel must surely die; Ellicott calls the belief universal among the Jews and stacks up the witnesses, chief among them the word that no man shall see God's face and live. Both go outside Israel for the same idea. Clarke has the fable of Jupiter and Semele, who asked to see his glory, saw it, and was struck dead by the effulgence; Ellicott adds Actæon and Psyche to her. Both quote the hymn of Callimachus to the same effect — that by the laws of Saturn a man who looks on any immortal, unless that god has chosen it, pays dearly for the sight.

The reassurance comes from a source the commentators cannot quite locate. Ellicott admits the text does not say how the intimation was given, and notes that here the Greek translators leave the Lord standing rather than altering it to the angel of the Lord. Gill offers a secret impulse on Gideon's spirit or a voice out of heaven, and cites Kimchi's suggestion that the angel, having ascended and seeing the man's terror, might himself have caused the voice to be heard — which he treats as further proof that this angel was Jehovah, the eternal Word. Keil and Delitzsch are certain the words were not the angel's parting speech but God's, spoken inwardly after the disappearance. Clarke draws the moral: the discovery was God's own doing, not the fruit of Gideon prying into forbidden mysteries, and therefore he would not die.

The altar is built on the spot, and Gill puts it on the top of the rock where the food had lain — the fire that came out of it having certified acceptance, and, he adds, promised that Midian would be consumed as quickly and as easily. On what the altar was for, the readings diverge. Keil and Delitzsch insist it was no place of sacrifice but a memorial and witness, standing until the book was written, of the revelation Gideon had received and of the proof that the Lord meant peace and not wrath toward Israel — an assurance which doubled as confirmation that he would beat Midian in God's strength. Ellicott agrees, citing the altar Ed, raised by the tribes across Jordan, as an instance of altars built to commemorate a great event or a divine appearance rather than to burn anything. Clarke, translating the name as the Lord is my peace or the peace of Jehovah, ties it to the words just spoken and reads them as prediction and not merely good wish — and then suggests that this altar is the very one mentioned a little later, named here by anticipation, which would make it a place of sacrifice after all. Ellicott closes with the company the name keeps: Jehovah-jireh, Jehovah-nissi, Jehovah-tsidkenu.
25:
The second word comes the same night as the first. Gill dates it to the night after the threshing-floor; Henry treats it as the correspondence kept up by another route, God speaking in a dream while Gideon was still full of what had passed and had told nobody — with the encouragement that God's visits, gratefully received, are graciously repeated: bid him welcome and he comes again. Ellicott, following Luther, warns against picturing a voice in the air and thinks it useless to ask how the intimation came, since a man cannot mistake God's voice. What it made plain was that Gideon must be an iconoclast before he could be a deliverer.

Keil and Delitzsch give the reason: he could not free Israel until he had purged his father's house of idolatry and sanctified his life and labour by a burnt offering. Henry works the thought harder. The new judge begins his government at home; grace raised both a reformer and a rescuer out of the household of a ringleader in idolatry; and Gideon's keeping away from that altar was not enough — he must pull it down, not, as bishop Hall notes, re-consecrate it, since God commands the monuments of superstition down before enjoining his own service. Two purposes Henry finds: to test the man's zeal before the field tested his courage, and to begin the reformation, sin being the cause and oppression its effect; one example might be copied by other towns.

What stood on the altar Ellicott insists on naming: not a grove but the Asherah — Baal the sun and the nature-goddess often confounded with Astarte were worshipped in company — and it stood on the altar, not beside it. No image of Baal is mentioned, so perhaps the sun was adored there without one while the Asherah — a bare wooden pillar, a gross emblem of nature-worship — was set on top. God being one, and therefore jealous of the easy blending of idolatries every polytheism allows, Baal's altar must come down before God's goes up. Henry cites bishop Patrick for taking the grove to mean the image in it, probably Ashtaroth, on the altar or close by.

The bullocks are the hard part of the verse. Keil and Delitzsch read two animals — the father's young bullock and an ox of seven years — and note that the first is never heard of again, which leaves its purpose obscure and has driven most commentators to suppose both were offered. Clarke guesses the second had been fattened for Baal, being so carefully distinguished from one of Joash's; and since the altar stood on Joash's land yet seems common property, the beast was likely reared at the villagers' charge — or why resent its going to Jehovah? Ellicott turns on the conjunction. Ewald reads even, making the word for second mean old; the Greek, the Vulgate and Luther read and, which he prefers, since two beasts' labour would not be too much for the night's work, and a seven-year-old would hardly be called a young bullock. The Chaldee has fattened seven years, perhaps glancing at the seven years of oppression; no age for burnt offerings was fixed by law; and why this one is the second nobody can say — an unexplained detail which he thinks shows the narrative is no legend. His conjecture: the first was Joash's and meant for Baal, the second Gideon's own, a votive beast kept fattening against the longed-for day, so that using it told him the day had come. Henry allots them differently: the young bullock for Gideon, the older for the sins of the people he was to rescue, peace being made with God before war on Midian, since till sin is pardoned nothing good is to be looked for. Beasts prepared for Baal, he adds, were turned to better use, the stronger dividing the spoil of the strong.
26:
The new altar goes where the old sign was given. Gill puts it on the crown of the rock where the food had been laid and the fire had broken out, close to the memorial already standing there, and thinks the ledge wide enough for both — for these were two altars and not one. The earlier was a monument, meant to last, and did; this one was for sacrifice and for the occasion only, the tabernacle being the proper place for offerings. Ellicott looks at the word for rock and finds it is neither of the two used a few verses back but maoz, a stronghold, probably the citadel of Ophrah; the Greek takes it for a place-name, and some copies read on the top of this mountain. Everywhere else in Hebrew the word belongs to poetry.

The phrase our version renders in the ordered place defeats everybody. Gill offers two senses — the spot where Gideon had been told to lay the flesh and the cakes, or else in the orderly fashion the law required, an altar of earth and unhewn stone built to carry wood and victim. Ellicott doubts both text and margin. The Hebrew is bammaarachah, and because the prefixed particle can mark the stuff a thing is built of, some translate it with the materials; the Jews were plainly unsure themselves, the Greek giving in the arrangement and the Vulgate on which you have before placed the sacrifice. His own sense is with the Asherah pillar hewn down and split into firewood.

That fuel is what Clarke stops over. He takes the Asherah for Astarte and supposes a wooden image of the goddess standing on Baal's altar, the pair of them well matched — Baal-peor answering to Priapus and Astarte to Venus, two impure idols fit to share one altar. Wood, he adds, is what early and rude peoples make their gods of, and still do: the islanders of the South Sea, the Indians of America, the people of Ceylon whose images of Budhoo are largely wooden, and the Scandinavians before them.

The irregularity of the whole proceeding was noticed long ago, and Ellicott lists what the Jews counted against it. The burnt offering was not made at Shiloh; no priest offered it; it was offered by night; and the fire was kindled with the unhallowed timber of an idol. God's command, he says, more than covered breaches of that kind, and in so rude a time, with the country in heathen hands, the Levitic order had become impossible at many points — men holding a direct commission from heaven being tacitly excused the outward rules that bound the nation.

Ten servants did the work. Gill explains the number both ways: they were men Gideon could order and also men he could trust, who like himself had never bowed the knee, and the night's business needed hands enough for dispatch — an altar to throw down, an idol to cut up, another altar to build, a victim to kill and offer. Ellicott reads the ten as evidence of his standing, and of an effort to keep his own household clean in an almost universal defection; the father's house he glosses as the Abi-ezrites, and remarks that many of the townsmen may have been Canaanite by race. Clarke infers from the fear that Joash was an idolater, and from the trusted servants that Gideon had kept the true faith and never bowed to the image. Keil and Delitzsch fix the timing and the motive together: the thing was done with those ten men in the night, and no doubt the very night the word came, because doing it by day meant facing his family and the townspeople.
28:
Morning shows them what the night has done. Gill has the townsmen out early at the place of the altar, the grove and the image, come to pay their first devotions; Ellicott notes that Eastern habits are early anyway, and that Baal-worship may well have included some greeting of the rising sun. Three things met them, on his reckoning — the wrecked altar, the stump of the felled Asherah, and a new altar with the remains of a burnt offering smoking on it. Keil and Delitzsch add the practical reason the evidence was still there: the bullock would not have burned away entirely. They also pause on the grammar, the passive taking an accusative in a construction not at all rare in the older Hebrew, and on the ambiguity of the next clause — the men who answered may be the enquirers themselves or the neighbours they questioned.

Which bullock had been offered, and why that one, divides them. Clarke ties the choice to the age: seven years old, calved about the time the Midianite oppression began, and killed now to signify that the servitude would expire with its life — the younger beast serving as a peace-offering and the older as the burnt offering. Ellicott reports the alternative, that Gideon offered both, the first for his household and the second for the nation, but doubts it, since the text says nothing about what became of the young bullock, and without an explicit order Gideon might well have hesitated to give the Lord an animal that had perhaps been vowed to Baal.

Finding the culprit took no time. Gill describes them amazed, unable to imagine who would dare anything so wicked; Keil and Delitzsch say they asked and sought and soon learned it was Gideon son of Joash. Clarke thinks they fastened on him the sooner because they knew he had never joined their idolatrous worship. Ellicott makes the same point at more length: we are not told that the servants gave their master away, but suspicion would naturally settle on a man so brave and so conspicuous a worshipper of Jehovah, and work needing that much effort and that many hands is seldom kept quiet. Gideon had proved himself what his name means, a hewer — and a man of that courage and patriotism must have stood nearly alone among a cringing and apostate people.

The demand made of his father is the ugly turn. Gill has the chief inhabitants meet and go in a body to Joash, their chief magistrate, to have justice done; Ellicott, who has already doubted whether these townsmen were Israelites at all, finds it hard to conceive that they were, and reads their sentence — bring out thy son, that he may die — as a stock formula of summary execution. Clarke explains their heat by their interest. Every man of them had a stake in keeping up rites that afforded him a good deal of sensual gratification; and that, he says, is why Baal and Ashtaroth would always draw more worshippers than the true God, their service being the better fitted to fallen nature.
31:
Joash answers the mob, and the answer is cleverer than it looks. Gill takes those he addresses to be his son's accusers, pressing for the young man to be handed over and killed; Ellicott finds the phrase genuinely obscure and thinks it may mean no more than the bystanders. What follows is a challenge with a doubled pronoun in it — will ye, ye, contend for Baal, and will ye save him? — which Keil and Delitzsch and Clarke both mark as emphatic, Clarke pointing to the lengthened verb forms that thicken the sense: will you plead in earnest, will you really rescue him? If he is a god, let him contend for himself, since it is his altar that has been thrown down.

Ellicott calls the speech extraordinarily bold and cunning, and thinks his son's courage may have stirred the father's conscience, perhaps after Gideon told him he had acted under divine direction. Joash saves him not by defending what he did but by counterfeiting a zeal so hot that doubting Baal's power to avenge himself becomes the blasphemy — an impiety monstrous enough to deserve instant death. Baal-worship is thus turned into the argument for leaving Baal's injury unavenged. And time was the whole point. Keil and Delitzsch resist the reading that makes till the morning mean before daybreak, in the sense of a summary execution, and attach the words elsewhere in the sentence; Ellicott takes the Hebrew, with the Greek, the Vulgate, the Syriac, the Arabic and the Chaldee, to mean before to-morrow's sun rises — that is, let us wait and see whether Baal will act — and remarks that in a popular tumult delay is safety. He knew, too, what the waiting would prove: among idolaters an act of open contempt that draws no thunder shakes the reverence of the worshippers. Aristophanes, Persius and Lucían all sneer at a Jupiter who cannot defend his own temple and his golden locks and beard; when Olaf had the great image of Odin destroyed, and when the high priest Coifi at Saxmundham rode at the Saxon idols in armour and on horseback, both forbidden him, and threw them down, the onlookers saw that nothing followed and the world went on, and were ready to turn Christian.

Clarke reaches the same conclusion by another road. Joash could not kill his son, and was satisfied the insult to Baal was real; if Baal were truly God he would right his own honour. The heathen thought so themselves, and Clarke produces two witnesses. Tacitus has Tiberius write to the consuls, over two knights accused of selling a statue of the deified Augustus with a garden and of swearing falsely by his name, that heaven was not decreed to his father in order to trap citizens, that an image sold along with houses and grounds is no wrong to religion, and that a false oath is a fraud on Jupiter — injuries done to the gods being the gods' own business. Livy reports the senators, displeased at a move to draw augurs from the commons, pretending the matter concerned the gods rather than themselves, and that the gods would see to it that their rites were not polluted.Keil and Delitzsch carry the scene one step past the rescue, to the name it left behind. Jerubbaal means let Baal contend, or let Baal decide, formed from the verb and the god's own name; and the taunt very soon became a title of honour, for once it was plain that Baal could do the man no harm the word was heard instead as Baal-fighter, one who had taken the god on. They add that a later book calls him Jerubbesheth, Bosheth being a standing nickname for Baal, of a piece with Ishbosheth standing in for Eshbaal.
32:
Out of the day came a name, and the three who handle it agree on its plain sense before differing about everything else. Clarke renders Jerubbaal let Baal contend. Ellicott adds two shades to that: the Hebrew phrasing is impersonal, so that Gideon got the name rather than his father conferred it — the Latin and Luther both take it so — and the form will also bear let it be striven with Baal, or Baal's antagonist, which he thinks helped the name catch on. He wonders besides whether something more allusive lies behind it, since the Palmyrene inscriptions show a deity called Jaribolos. Gill simply has Joash give his son the title.

The name did not come down to us intact. Clarke translates the substitution that a later book makes — bosheth, confusion or ignominy, put in the place of baal, lord, so that the man now contends against shame. Ellicott explains the habit behind the change. Bosheth means shame, that shameful thing, and served as a term of scorn for Baal; the Jews read the law against so much as naming other gods literally enough to disfigure every such name they had inherited, which is how Esh-baal and Merib-baal, the sons of Saul, reach us as Ishbosheth and Mephibosheth, and it is part of what the ancients meant when they charged the nation with contumelia numinum. He enters one caution, from Ewald and others: baal and bosheth may both have carried less offensive associations at an earlier date, and there was, after all, a Baal among the ancestors of Saul himself.

The last question is whether Gideon turns up in a pagan historian. Gill reports the identification with Jerombalus, priest of the god Jevo, from whom the ancient Phoenician writer Sanchoniatho is said — on Philo Byblius's authority — to have drawn the substance of what he wrote about the Jews. Ellicott has the Greek translators spelling the name Hierobalos, and quotes Eusebius, drawing on the same Philo, for Sanchoniatho of Berytus, a writer he praises for accuracy in Jewish history and geography, being helped by Hierombalos, priest of the god Iao; some, he says, have supposed the reference is to Gideon. Clarke will have none of it. The history of Sanchoniatho is probably Porphyry's own forgery, and worth no credit whatever.
33:
Why the invasion came when it did is disputed. Clarke thinks the raiders heard what Gideon had done, took it for a first bid for liberty, and formed a general league against Israel. Gill denies the connection: this was their usual season for crossing into Canaan, harvest time, as Gideon's threshing shows, and they came as they had for years, to carry off the increase of the earth. Ellicott agrees it was the annual raid, and adds that thousands besides Gideon had been reaping and threshing in secret as soon as the wheat was ripe. Henry allows the first as a possibility — that they came to plead for Baal and make his altar a pretext — but prefers the second, and notes that they were expected while Gideon was at the winepress, God having raised the deliverer up in time.

Where they camped they agree. Keil and Delitzsch have them cross the Jordan near Beisan and pitch in the valley of Jezreel; Ellicott, taking the fords by Bethshean, would put them not in the broad plain but in the trough between Gilboa and Little Hermon, and notes the meaning of the name, God's sowing. Henry notices that nobody cared or dared to hold so important a pass, and that their headquarters lay in the heart of Manasseh, near Gideon's own town. Long success, feeble opposition and heavy plunder had made them eager and confident, he says; but the measure of their iniquity was full, and men who had spoiled so long must now be spoiled, gathered like sheaves to the floor for Gideon to thresh.

The muster Henry finds remarkable twice over. The men of Abiezer, who lately raged at him for pulling down Baal's altar and demanded his life as a criminal's, now saw their error, came bravely to his help, and took him for their commander — so suddenly, Henry observes, can God turn the hearts of idolaters and persecutors. And tribes as far off as Asher and Naphtali, strangers to him, obeyed the summons and sent their best men; furthest from the danger, they reckoned that if their neighbours were overrun their own turn came next, and were forward against a common enemy.

On the signs Gideon afterwards asked for, Henry is gentle with him. Perhaps he wanted them less for himself than for his followers, or to learn whether this was the hour; at bottom it means Lord, I believe, help thou my unbelief. Coming back for a second sign he prefaced it with an apology — let not thine anger be hot against me — which Henry sets beside Abraham's O let not the Lord be angry, and I will speak. See, he says, how tender God is of weak believers, that the bruised reed be not broken nor the smoking flax quenched. The reversal answered an objection: wool takes up whatever moisture falls, so the first trial might be called natural, though the quantity wrung out answered that. Dr Fuller's remark on it is that heaven's real miracles will endure turning, being inside and outside both alike. Dew is from the Lord and tarrieth not for man, yet here God hearkened to a man about the dew as once about the sun, which shows it falls by providence and not by chance. The meaning Henry finds is a question and its answer: could God tell a small fleece of Israel from the vast floor of Midian? He could. Would the dew of grace fall on Gideon in particular? The fleece is wet. Would God be as the dew to all Israel? All the ground is wet. The fleece has since been read as the Jewish nation, watered while the world lay dry and now dry as the heath while the nations round are a watered garden; and in one congregation, he ends, one soul is the moistened fleece, another the dry ground.
34:
The verb is the thing here, and three of them stop on it. Gill records that the Hebrew says the Spirit clothed Gideon, and rules out one construction of the gift: not the spirit of prophecy, whatever Maimonides may say in calling this the first degree of it, but a spirit of fortitude and courage, as the Targum has it, arming him with zeal and might for an attempt on so vast an invading force. Keil and Delitzsch press the same figure harder — the Spirit descended and laid itself about him like a coat of mail, so that in its strength he was neither to be wounded nor beaten. Ellicott collects the other men the phrase is used of, Othniel and Jephthah and Samson before all, and follows it out of the Old Testament into the New, where the disciples are to be clothed with power from on high and believers have put on Christ. Clarke says the least and the same: Gideon was endued with preternatural courage and wisdom.

Then the horn. Ellicott identifies it as the shophar, the ram's horn, and reads the blast as the start of a second obedience — the first call Gideon had already answered by destroying the Baal-worship at Ophrah, and this one commits him to delivering his country. Keil and Delitzsch simply note that the trumpet summoned Israel to battle with the enemy.

The summons went further than the sound could carry. Gill explains the two stages: the horn reached the Abiezrites near at hand, and messengers carried the appeal to the rest of Manasseh — his own tribe — further off. He rejects the notion that both halves of the tribe are meant, taking it that only the half within Jordan answered. Ellicott sees in the loyalty of Gideon's own clan the warrant for asking wider help, and reads the roll with an eye to old grievances. Asher partly redeemed a reputation tarnished by an earlier defection, not lingering this time among the sands of Accho or the rocks of the Tyrian Ladder; Zebulun and Naphtali distinguished themselves again, as they had in the campaign against Jabin. Two names are missing, and he accounts for both. Issachar bowed his shoulder to the yoke as before, perhaps because holding the plain of Jezreel — the battle-field of Palestine — was bad for a tribe's independence and strength. Ephraim was not asked at all: fierce, haughty, and jealous of any leader not of their own blood, they would likely have rebuffed him, and Gideon did not risk it.
36:
Whom Gideon addressed Gill settles first: not, as Ben Gersom held, a prophet standing by, but God in prayer, which is Abarbinel's view. Ellicott reads the hesitation as a measure of the crisis rather than a lapse — the man had already proved his faith, but he could see that human strength would be useless against so countless a horde, and wanted fresh heart for a dangerous errand. Clarke calls him very bold and God very condescending, and suspects the request itself was prompted by the Spirit.

Gill locates the experiment on the threshing-floor where Gideon had been working and the angel had first appeared, open to the sky so that dew could fall freely. Ellicott corrects a habit of the painters, who make the fleece a whole sheepskin — a mistake he traces to the Vulgate and to Luther's rendering — and then does something braver: he admits the first sign might have come about naturally. That, he argues, is exactly what shows the narrative honest, since Gideon would hardly have asked for a proof he knew to be no proof. Bishop Hervey's citation of Lord Bacon supplies the physics — sailors used to hang fleeces over the sides of their ships at night and wring fresh water from them by morning — and anyone may see wool caught on a hedge still glittering when the leaves about it have dried. The psalm that speaks of rain coming down into a fleece of wool uses this same Hebrew word, he notes, though there the sense may rather be mown grass.

The trial answered generously. Keil and Delitzsch have Gideon up early, pressing and squeezing the fleece until he had a vessel full of water out of it, so heavily had the dew fallen on it while the ground round about stayed dry; Ellicott identifies the vessel by the Hebrew name it shares with the lordly dish of the earlier song. Gill takes the miracle as granted for the confirming of Gideon's faith and the encouragement of the men with him.

What the sign might mean beyond itself is where Clarke spends his space, and he spends it on Origen's eighth homily, reproducing the scheme entire. The fleece is the Jewish nation: wet while all around is dry, that nation favoured with the law and the prophets; dry while all around is watered, that nation cast off for refusing the Gospel and the Gentiles brought in. The fleece on the threshing-floor is the people of Judea, winnowed and fanned by the Gospel; the dew wrung into the bowl is the doctrine of Christianity drawn out of the Jewish writings, figured beforehand when Christ poured water into a basin and washed his disciples' feet. The homilist ends by saying he has now wrung this water from the fleece of the book of Judges, hopes to wring more from Kings and from Isaiah or Jeremiah, has taken it into the basin of his own heart where its true sense was conceived, and would wash his brethren's feet, that they may walk in the preparation of the Gospel of peace. Clarke's verdict is mixed and worth having whole: some will think all this trifling, yet scarcely a pious mind can read the homily without drinking in a measure of the same spirit, so much sincerity and unction runs through it; he does not follow the method himself and therefore cannot recommend it; and of dealers in such small wares, he ends, we have many that imitate Benjamin Keach and few that come nigh to Origen.
39:
Gideon asks a second time on the morning after the first answer, Gill notes, and in the same way as before. Keil and Delitzsch explain why he needed to. The first proof was not quite conclusive, since wool will draw dew when things beside it stay dry, so he ventured to ask for the opposite arrangement — a dry fleece on wet ground — and God granted that too. The request, they insist, did not come from any distrust of what God had promised; it came from the weakness of the flesh, which cramps the strength of the spirit's faith and leaves God's servants anxious and downcast until he relieves them by another display of his power. Gideon knew himself, and knew his own strength was not equal to what lay before him.

The apology he prefaced it with catches Ellicott's ear twice. The wording, he observes, is Abraham's, repeated as it stands; and the noun our version renders anger is literally nose — Hebrew being a picturesque language, and the dilating nostril so regular a mark of rage that the word for the feature became the word for the passion, as it still is across many Eastern tongues.

The night did what was asked of it. Gill remarks only that night is the season when dew falls; Keil and Delitzsch record the outcome flatly, the fleece dry and dew over all the ground; Ellicott points out that a result of that kind, running clean against natural circumstance, could have come from nothing but direct interposition.

Then he draws a line against reading more into it. The dew can of course be allegorised as the sign of grace, so that the first night shows Israel replenished with God's love while everything round about is dry, and the second shows God manifesting himself in his people's weakness and desolation while the nations flourish. St Ambrose took the same road, finding in the fleece full of dew the Hebrew nation with the mystery of Christ hidden inside it, and in the dry fleece that mystery carried out to the whole world and the nation left without it; and one might as easily make the threshing-floor a type of the universal Church. Such applications of a plain narrative, Ellicott says, are precarious to say the least — and he thinks even less of Ewald's conceit that the fleece stands for Gideon's own temper, cool amid the general passion and dry amid the general damp of fear.
